newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Guatemala promised $1.9 billion in international aid.
newsitem.headline: Guatemala promised $1.9 billion in international aid.

text.p: The international community pledged over $1.9 billion on Wednesday to help Guatemala rebuild after three decades of civil war.

The Guatemalan government had calculated it needed some $2.5 billion for rebuilding programmes, but Finance Minister Jose Alejandro Arevalo said the aid would go a long way towards solving the Central American nation's problems.
"I wish to express great satisfaction at the international community's contribution to our development," Arevalo told a news conference after a two-day donor conference in Brussels.
"We have a lot to do and this will ensure we make the right start," he added.

The Inter-American Development Bank, organisers of the conference, said international organisations and individual nations had pledged $1.9 billion to Guatemala over the next four years in the form of grants and soft loans.
A breakdown of the pledged contributions was not immediately available.

The conference was called to promote plans to implement an ambitious peace treaty signed on December 29 between the Guatemalan government and leftist Guatemalan National Revolutionary Unit (URNG) rebels.
Under the peace agreements, the Guatemalan army is to cut its numbers and about 3,000 guerrillas from the URNG are to go to assembly points, disarm and be integrated into civilian life.
Donors at the conference stressed the need for Guatemala to adopt strict measures to swiftly bring about macro-economic stability and particular emphasis was placed on broadening the tax base.
Guatemala has said it is committed to increasing revenue from taxes by 50 percent from 1995 levels by 2000 and has already raised value added tax (VAT) to 10 percent as a first step.

The World Bank told the meeting that real gross domestic product (GDP) growth is expected to increase from 3.1 percent in 1996 to six percent in 1999-2000 with total investment projected to rise from 15 percent to 20 percent.
The bank praised Guatemala's efforts to reduce public spending, noting that the public sector deficit decreased from one percent of GDP in 1995 to an estimated 0.7 percent last year.
The external debt service ratio (as a percentage of exports of goods and services) remained low at about 11 percent, it said.
However, the bank noted that 58 percent of Guatemalans -- including 98 percent of its indigenous population -- was classified as "poor" with nearly half "extremely poor".
Donor countries stressed their desire to see that aid pledged would go towards projects that would bring the population above the poverty line.
